title: How do migrating birds find their way?
hook: The sun, the stars and a magnetic sense that science is still decoding.
summary: Migrating birds use several compasses: the sun, the stars, which they learn to read, and Earth’s magnetic field, sensed by a mechanism that is still being studied.
cardText: They carry more than one compass: the sun, the stars, which they learn to recognise, and Earth’s magnetic field, which they sense in a way scientists are still working out.

cardBlocks.text: Sailors of old steered by the sun, the stars and a compass. Migrating birds use all three. In the 1950s, researchers showed that birds orient themselves by the sun and, at night, by the stars. In 1967, Emlen watched indigo buntings orient under the artificial sky of a planetarium, and it turned out that this star compass is not inborn: it is learned.

The third compass is magnetic. In 1966, European robins in a cage changed direction when scientists shifted magnetic north with electric coils. Today the leading explanation is that a molecule in the eyes called cryptochrome reacts to light in a way that depends on the direction of the magnetic field. But many details, such as how this becomes a signal to the brain, are still unclear.
Migrating birds combine the sun, learned star patterns and a magnetic sense whose workings are still being studied.

deepDiveBlocks.text: Knowing which way is north is not enough. In the 1950s, the researcher Gustav Kramer proposed that an animal travelling beyond familiar ground needs two things: a map, to know where it is relative to its goal, and a compass, to pick a direction and hold it.
Building a fully working star compass can take two to three weeks. It is especially useful near the magnetic equator, where the birds’ magnetic compass becomes ambiguous and fails.
A traveller that passes through Brazil

The rufa red knot (Calidris canutus rufa) breeds in the Canadian Arctic and spends the northern winter in the southern hemisphere. Some birds stay on the coast of Maranhão in northern Brazil; others fly on to Tierra del Fuego, stopping in southern Brazil, at places such as Lagoa do Peixe, to feed and rest. From Brazil to their next stop, Delaware Bay in the United States, is roughly 8,000 kilometres. In 2019, a tagged female flew that stretch nonstop: 8,289 km in 14 days from Lagoa do Peixe.
